notes: TOWN LIFE · what walking gives that a list cannot ('walking
around versus picking from a list is superficial').
presence · who is physically AT a place, by month + weather.
First matching entry wins. away:true = the usual person is
NOT there (absence is information too). sight = the line as
you come near; talk = the line at E when no activity fits.
months use 0=Sep .. 9=Jun; omit = all. wx omit = any weather.
overheard · lines caught crossing Main Street, per season.
moments · route-only encounters at spots BETWEEN places — the
bridge, the boardwalk, the hill path. Walking past triggers
them; the month list gates them; once:true spends them for
the whole run. gives{} grants without costing the week —

presence.sight: Del's slip is empty — the whole fleet is out on the run. The nets are gone from the rail.
presence.talk: Nobody on the dock but gulls. During the run the dock is just the place the boats aren't.

presence.sight: Del is on the dock in oilskins, doubling every line, unhurried, like the storm is a customer he has served before.
presence.talk: Del points with his chin at the doubled lines. 'She'll pull tonight.' That is the whole conversation, and it is enough.

presence.sight: No smoke up the draw. Boyd winters lower down, wherever that is. The woods keep his side of it.
presence.talk: The trail up is churned mud and quiet. Boyd finds you in winter, not the other way round.

presence.sight: The school is shut for summer, windows papered from inside. The flag line still clinks.
presence.talk: Locked. Even the building looks like it's on vacation.

presence.sight: The cannery is running flat out — steam off the roof vents, trucks nose to tail, the line's rain-on-tin roar.
presence.talk: Manny, in passing, at speed: 'Run season. Talk in December.' He means it kindly. He means it.

presence.sight: The line is down for the winter. Manny is somewhere inside painting machinery its annual coat of gray.
presence.talk: Manny shows you what a salmon canner looks like with its skin off. He is happier now than in October, and says the opposite.

presence.sight: Storm rules: the cafe is full of fishermen not fishing, and the windows are gray and streaming.
presence.talk: Ruth has given up on tables and gone to a system of general gravity. The coffee is free past the third cup because counting stopped.

presence.sight: Fir garlands on the church door, and the notice board is all Christmas — the pageant, the candle service, whose kitchen wants pies.
presence.talk: Inside, two women are arguing about the pageant's sheep costumes with the intensity of a border dispute.

presence.sight: The light in Estelle's window that faces the bar is lit in daylight. Storm days it is always lit.
presence.talk: She does not answer the door in a storm. The light answers for her.

presence.sight: Lanterns are already strung out on the flats — the minus tide has the whole town up before the sun.
presence.talk: Boot prints by the hundred, heading out. If you want the flats this week, the year menu knows the way.

fall: '—forty cases an hour, she said, and I said not on that belt—'
'—new kid. Staying with Maria Rocha. The daughter's boy—' — and then they see you, and smile, unembarrassed.
'—says the run's early. His knee says. His KNEE, Alma—'
'—the President, shot? You heard the radio same as—' — and the street is quiet a moment, even the gulls.
'—won't sell the boat. He'll sink at the mooring first, and Del would tell you the same—'
winter: '—three days the power was out and she STILL had bread rising, I don't know how—'
'—lumber all down Agate Beach, first come first served is what the law is going to amount to—'
'—the road's under at the slough again. Under. Again. Every year we act surprised—'
'—asked the Rocha kid to mind the store Tuesday. Sharp, that one. Knows the whole delivery list—'
'—Estelle's light was on all through the blow. All through it. Somebody should—' — and the voices drop.
spring: '—herring in the bay like I never seen. Even the lazy gulls are fat—'
'—painted her hull the same green his father used. Sentimental as a post, that man—'
'—the school wants the field for baseball and the Grange wants it for the fair, so that's July spoken for—'
'—berries early this year up Deer Creek, but you didn't hear it from me—'
summer: '—Ferris wheel. On the CANNERY lot. Manny's beside himself, you'd think they'd parked it on his mother—'
'—fortune teller read Ruth's cards and Ruth won't say a word about it, which tells you plenty—'
'—one more month and the Rocha kid's a year in. Feels longer. Feels like the kid's always been here—'
'—longest day Saturday. The Silvas do the beach fire. Everyone. Yes, you too, new kid—'

moments.line: A heron owns the river bridge rail this morning. You stop. It stays. You both watch the water pretend to be in a hurry. It counts to something, knowing this.

gives.journal: The heron on the bridge rail does not move for anyone. The river does the moving.

moments.line: On the boardwalk between the dock and the cannery: a fish knife, dropped, good steel going to rust. You know whose it is by the whipping on the handle. Del takes it back without a word, but the look holds a beat longer than his looks do.
Swallows are building under the school eaves, mud beak-load by beak-load. You watch the whole shift change. Nobody teaches this class.

gives.journal: Swallows came back to the school eaves the same week as last year. Iris says they always do. Same week. Always.

moments.line: From the hill path above town, in winter light, you can see the whole of Salmonberry at once — every roof you know, smoke standing straight up from each one, the bay holding it all in one gray hand.

gives.journal: From the hill you can see every house whose kitchen you know. That is a kind of map they don't sell.

moments.line: The cannery cat — enormous, scarred, employed — falls into step beside you for exactly the length of the fence, then sits, shift over. You have been escorted.

gives.journal: The cannery cat walks you the fence line and not a step further. Union rules, Manny says.

moments.line: Round the side of the church, fresh flowers on one grave in the winter rain, tucked low against the wind. The stone's date is nineteen years ago this month. You are near enough to Estelle's to see her porch from here.
The storm has put a dory on the beach path — holed, green, hull-up, a name half sanded off the transom. Del will know it. Everyone will know it. Nobody will say it first.
The smelt are running the river mouth, a silver argument a yard wide. Two kids you know from school are netting them with a bedsheet, badly, joyfully. You are lent a corner of the sheet.
The show's roustabouts walk an honest-to-God pony down Main Street to the cannery lot, and the town finds reasons to be on porches. The pony accepts all tribute.

gives.journal: In June a pony walked down Main Street and the whole town pretended it wasn't watching. The pony knew better.
